title: Building Michelson Interferometer
summary: Built a Michelson interferometer and chased the alignment until the fringes finally made the path difference visible.
description: This build was an exercise in patience as much as optics. A beamsplitter divided the light into two perpendicular arms, mirrors sent the beams back, and the recombined light produced interference only when the geometry stopped fighting us. The project taught me how quickly a clean diagram becomes a sensitive physical instrument once screws, tables, and alignment errors enter the room.

field_notes.question: Can a tabletop setup make path difference visible as a real interference pattern?
field_notes.built: A two-arm Michelson interferometer with a beamsplitter, mirrors, and a recombined beam path.
field_notes.friction: Alignment drift and tiny mirror adjustments mattered more than the simplified diagram suggests.
field_notes.learned: Optical instruments reward patience: the signal appears only after the mechanical details behave.

title: Constructing Cloud Chamber with Peltier Disks
summary: Built a compact Peltier-cooled cloud chamber to make ionizing radiation leave visible tracks.
description: The goal was to turn an invisible event into something the eye could catch. The chamber used Peltier disks to create the cold region needed for supersaturated vapor, then tested whether the thermal gradient stayed stable enough for particle tracks. The hard part was less glamorous than the idea: heat removal, condensation, and keeping the chamber behavior steady.

field_notes.question: Can a small Peltier setup create the temperature gradient needed for particle tracks?
field_notes.built: A compact cloud chamber with cooled plates, insulation, and a visible observation volume.
field_notes.friction: The temperature drop was only useful when heat was carried away fast enough.
field_notes.learned: Radiation detection is also thermal engineering; the tracks depend on the cooling details.

images.caption: Temperature check while tuning the cooling stack.
Top view of the chamber before closing the observation volume.

title: Developing Soft Robotic Actuators
summary: Tested soft actuators that respond to electric fields, magnets, water, and pressure instead of rigid linkages.
description: This project treated motion as a materials problem. We explored dielectric elastomer actuators, electrochemical actuation, magnetic actuation, hydraulic response, and water-sensitive mechanisms, comparing how each material system moved, failed, or demanded a different kind of control. It made soft robotics feel less like a single technique and more like a family of compromises.

field_notes.question: How many ways can a soft material be persuaded to move?
field_notes.built: A set of actuator samples using electric, magnetic, hydraulic, and osmotic responses.
field_notes.friction: Each mechanism had its own failure mode: sealing, stiffness, response time, or control.
field_notes.learned: Soft robotics is less about one perfect actuator and more about matching material behavior to the task.

tech_stack: Soft Robotics, Materials, Actuation, Experimental Physics

title: Star Tracker
summary: Built a microcontroller-based star-tracker prototype that translated sensor readings and celestial coordinates into motor movement.
description: The star tracker began as a bridge between celestial coordinates and a physical mount. An ESP32 gathered orientation data from MPU sensors, synchronized time using NTP, and computed coordinates such as right ascension and declination. Those values were passed to an Arduino Mega for stepper-motor control. The prototype worked, but the full mount exposed unresolved problems in sensor noise, torque, and stability, which became the most useful part of the project.

field_notes.question: Can a small embedded system turn sky coordinates into a moving telescope mount?
field_notes.built: An ESP32 and Arduino Mega prototype linking sensors, time sync, coordinate calculations, and stepper motors.
field_notes.friction: The prototype exposed sensor noise, torque limits, and stability problems before the full mount could be finished.
field_notes.learned: A working electronics chain is only half the system; mechanics and noise decide whether tracking is trustworthy.

title: Stochastic Modeling for Elevator Systems Efficiency
summary: Modelled elevator demand with Poisson arrivals to test how control choices change waiting time and efficiency.
description: This honours project used Python simulations to treat elevator traffic as a stochastic system rather than a fixed schedule. Passenger arrivals were modelled with Poisson processes, then different control strategies were tested under uncertainty. The work became a way to think about everyday infrastructure as a probabilistic physics-and-systems problem.

field_notes.question: How does random passenger demand change what counts as an efficient elevator strategy?
field_notes.built: Python simulations using Poisson arrivals and rule-based elevator control strategies.
field_notes.friction: A strategy that looked efficient in one traffic pattern could behave poorly under another.
field_notes.learned: Efficiency is a distribution, not a single number; uncertainty has to be part of the model.

title: Studying Standing Sound Waves using Schlieren Imaging
summary: Used schlieren imaging to make invisible density changes in air visible, from heat plumes to standing sound waves.
description: Schlieren imaging became a way to watch air behave like a material. The setup revealed refractive-index changes caused by heat, smoke, and sound. The standing-wave work connected the optical method back to wave physics: pressure variations that are normally abstract became visible as changing structure in the image.

field_notes.question: Can an optical setup reveal pressure, heat, and flow patterns that are normally invisible?
field_notes.built: A schlieren imaging setup used to observe heat plumes, smoke motion, and standing sound waves.
field_notes.friction: Small changes in alignment and lighting changed how much of the density structure appeared.
field_notes.learned: Good visualization is not decoration; it changes what questions can be asked.
